title: The Evening Brief: Off-field stories close out a quiet sports night
dek: Inter Milan finalized its signing of Curtis Jones, Messi drew an MLS fine for slapping an opponent, and a second night of WNBA court disruptions brought a lifetime ban, while the day's larger institutional stories, the Times verdict and the Timberwolves sale, stood unchanged from the afternoon.
author: GoCheckMySports
key_fact: The day's defining stories were institutional rather than competitive: a defamation verdict against The New York Times, an ownership change atop the Timberwolves and Lynx, and a second consecutive night of WNBA game disruptions.
bottom_line: The day's competitive news, England's dominant Test win, Curtis Jones's move to Inter Milan, and Messi's MLS fine, sat alongside three larger institutional stories: a $9.25 million defamation verdict against The New York Times, Marc Stad's $4.5 billion acquisition of controlling interest in the Timberwolves and Lynx from co-chairman Marc Lore, and a second consecutive night of objects thrown onto WNBA courts. The Times verdict marks the organization's first U.S. defamation loss in more than 50 years, with an appeal still possible. The Stad transaction and Alex Rodriguez's expanded governance roles remain subject to NBA approval. Watch the two remaining Tests between England and Pakistan, the Times' next legal move, the NBA's approval decision, and whether Chicago authorities identify those responsible for Friday's WNBA disruption.
body: The evening added two on-field transactions and one further round of WNBA disruptions to a day that was otherwise shaped by courtrooms and ownership offices. Inter Milan completed its signing of Curtis Jones from Liverpool, and Lionel Messi was fined by MLS for slapping an opponent during Inter Miami's draw with Philadelphia Union. Neither changes the larger picture set earlier in the day: a federal jury's $9.25 million defamation verdict against The New York Times and Marc Stad's takeover of the Minnesota Timberwolves and Lynx remain the day's most consequential stories.

Inter Milan signed Curtis Jones for €35m total, €30m upfront plus €5m in add-ons, on a contract running through 2031. The move ends a negotiation that stretched across the summer, after Inter's verbal €25m offer in June was rejected by Liverpool, and closes Jones's 16-year association with the club after 228 appearances. Separately, MLS fined Messi after he slapped Philadelphia Union's Quinn Sullivan during Inter Miami's 2-2 draw at Subaru Park on Wednesday. The league did not disclose the fine amount. Messi said Sullivan had elbowed him first; the referee intervened after Sullivan reacted.

On the cricket side, England's innings-and-103-run win over Pakistan at Headingley, the opening result of Joe Root's second captaincy stint, still leads the series 1-0 with two Tests remaining, as reported this morning.

The WNBA's spectator disruptions extended into a second consecutive night. Objects were thrown onto the court during Chicago Sky versus Golden State Valkyries on Friday, forcing a stoppage in the third quarter, following a similar incident during Atlanta Dream versus Los Angeles Sparks on Thursday. A male spectator at the Los Angeles game was caught by arena security and will receive a lifetime ban from attending WNBA matches; it remains unclear whether those responsible for the Chicago incident have been identified. Sky guard Natasha Cloud responded publicly, calling the men involved "lame" and "weird." The reporting notes that similar incidents occurred last season between July and August, when a meme-coin group claimed responsibility and said the disruptions were meant to protest the league's policy on transgender athletes; the WNBA states there are no transgender athletes currently competing in the league.

On the Marc Stad transaction, the reporting is precise about what changed hands: Stad acquired the majority stake held by co-chairman Marc Lore, who together with Alex Rodriguez had invested in the Minnesota franchises in 2021 at a $1.5 billion valuation with an agreement to purchase the team in full, and who assumed full control of the basketball teams last year. The combined deal values the Timberwolves and Lynx at $4.5 billion, the fourth-largest NBA franchise sale on record. Rodriguez is increasing his investment and expanding his governance roles, pending NBA approval, to serve as co-chairman, Governor of the Lynx, and alternate Governor of the Timberwolves.

The reporting does not say why the Times chose not to make further changes to its March 2023 article beyond the June 2023 amendment, nor does it say what legal grounds the network of disruptions at WNBA games shares beyond the claimed protest motive from last season's meme-coin group. Those gaps remain open rather than resolved.
No desk boards were available this run, so nothing here is checked against a league feed; all figures come from the day's published stories.

The coming days carry several specific checkpoints. England and Pakistan have two Tests remaining in their three-match series. The New York Times is reviewing its legal options after the $9.25 million verdict, with an appeals path still open. Marc Stad's deal and Alex Rodriguez's expanded governance roles await NBA approval. Chicago authorities have not yet said whether they have identified those responsible for Friday's court disruption, and further WNBA incidents, or their absence, will indicate whether the pattern from last season is repeating.
